To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
shear stress enhances oxidation of VWF methionines in the A1, A2, and A3 domains.
shear stress accelerates the oxidation of key methonine residues in the largest VVF multimers, rendering them hyperfunctional and resistant proteolysis by the VWF-cleaving protease ADAMTS13.
neutrophil-derived oxidants oxidize VWF in a shear-dependent fashion, rendering it more functional and protease resistant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of VWF oxidation in hemostasis and the role of oxidative stress in VWF-mediated thrombosis.
the mechanisms by which VWF is activated by shear stress and oxidants, and the consequences of this activation on platelet adhesion.
the mechanisms by which VWF is activated by inflammation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

shear stress enhances the oxidation of VWF by HOCl, which results in the oxidation of several methionine residues within the A1A3 domain, and the accumulation of these oxidized forms of VWF in the largest VWD forms, resulting in the hyperfunctional state of these oxidized VWF multimers.
shear stress-induced oxidation of VWF is a novel mechanism by which inflammation can alter hemostasis and contribute to thrombotic disease.
neutrophils, through the release of oxidants, are capable of altering the structure and function of VWF.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
shear stress and inflammation are two important factors that regulate the functional state of VWF.

neutrophil-derived oxidants, such as HOCl, can inhibit ADAMTS13 activity and render VWF resistant to proteolysiss, and at the same time, they can alter the VWF molecule in a manner to render it hyperfunctional and resistant proteolysis.

neutrophils may contribute to the hypercoagulability of inflammation by oxidizing VVF, rendering it hyperfunctional and resistant proteolysis by the VWF-cleaving protease ADAMTS13.
